newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa pipe makers eye regional gas industry.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa pipe makers eye regional gas industry.

text.p: South Africa's beleaguered steel tube and pipe manufacturing industry is pinning its long-term survival on the planned multi-billion rand development of regional oil and gas pipelines.
In the short-term, it is banking on increasing the structural steel market in the construction sector and getting more contracts to supply pipelines for water projects in Africa.

These contracts will be undertaken by a consortia of existing pipe and tube manufacturing firms, resulting in widescale rationalisation to change the face of the previously overtraded and uncompetitive industry.

Association of Steel Tube and Pipe Manufacturers of South Africa (ASTPM) executive director Martin Done told a special briefing of the Department of Trade and Industry that the industry had privately funded its own cluster study in order to ensure its survival.
Outdated technology, dwindling exports and the removal of export incentives had plunged the industry into a crisis and it was clear that drastic action was needed, he said.
"The consequences for the South African economy would be very serious if the steel tube and pipe manufacturing sector were to decline further," Done told the briefing.

"There is tremendous over-capacity, particularly in the large bore manufacturing sector, but in order to justify the upgrading of plant and equipment you would need to actually rationalise and get rid of a lot of the over-capacity, otherwise you could not justify spending 200 million rand ($44.3 million) or whatever it is going to cost," he added.
He said there was a need for the adoption of new technology and rationalisation if the industry wanted to be efficient and prove competitive with the rest of the world.

"Certain sectors are due for a major shake-up if we are going to be able to supply the gas pipeline market. We would certainly need upgrading of technology, new grades of steel, more sophisticated coatings, corrosion protection systems and so on."

The cluster study - an in depth analysis of the industry - found that the greatest potential for future growth lay in the development of regional oil and gas pipelines from offshore gas fields in Namibia and Mozambique as well as future developments from Sasol Gas and state-owned Mossgas.
Done said the country's 10 major tube and pipe manufacturers could club together to form a consortia to undertake these contracts although some work could be done individually.

Although Namibia's Kudu and Mozambique's Pande gas fields were not expected to be up and running for another 10 to 15 years, ASTPM had already started work with steel manufacturer Iscor Ltd to supply the stronger grades of steel needed for pipelines which were not made locally yet.
"But there could be something a lot sooner in maybe three years time," Done said, referring to plans by the Industrial Development Corporation to build an iron reduction plant in Maputo.

"This would require a gas pipeline from Pande down to Maputo and a slurry line from Phalaborwa to Maputo, which would probably require a consortium because it is so big," Done said. ASTPM members include Murray and Roberts Holdings Ltd's Hall Longmore and Co, Dorbyl Ltd's Steel Pipe Industries, Barlows Plc's Brollo Africa and Macsteel Tube and Pipe.

Done said ASTPM was also promoting the use of steel tube and pipe for construction. The industry only supplied four percent of the construction market with structural hollow sections to replace conventional steel sections and concrete and timber structures compared to the market average of 20 percent abroad.
"We also believe that we should be getting a lot more business from Africa.

"There is a tremendous amount of bulk water pipelines being installed in Sub-Saharan Africa and we are not getting our fair share of that. So we are going to have a joint initiative to develop and obtain a bigger share," he said.
